groups.title: I am a child
groups.description: Big pictures and stories to help you stay safe.

picture.alt: Children walking together along a village path to school with bags on their backs: Kadiatu in a light blue headscarf carrying books and waving, Abu with round glasses and a hearing aid, Fatmata in her blue and white uniform waving, and Ibrahim in his white shirt and blue tie skipping ahead

groups.title: I am a parent or carer
groups.description: How to keep your children safe and listen to them.

picture.alt: A family at home in front of their zinc-roof house: Haja the grandmother holding a cup of tea, Isatu the mother in a blue head tie welcoming you with an open hand, and Mohamed the father in a blue cap leaning on the doorframe

groups.title: I am a community elder
groups.description: Your role in keeping the children of your community safe.

picture.alt: Community elders at the barray, an open shelter with a zinc roof: Pa Alimamy, the chief with a white beard and white kufi, sits on a bench and speaks with his hand raised, beside Ya Bintu the women's leader in a tall blue head wrap, while a small group of people sit and listen

groups.title: Chickens and quail
groups.description: Housing, feeding and keeping birds healthy.

picture.alt: In a family compound beside a zinc-roof house, Kemoh in his blue cap holds a bowl of grain and scatters a handful to local hens, a black hen, a white hen and little yellow chicks that peck around his feet.

groups.title: Rabbits
groups.description: Housing, breeding, feeding and young rabbits.

picture.alt: Aminata kneels on the grass and holds out a bunch of fresh green leaves. A white rabbit nibbles them while a brown rabbit and a grey rabbit hop closer. Their raised hutch stands behind.

groups.title: Milk and dairy cows
groups.description: Milking, clean milk, yoghurt and cheese.

picture.alt: Pa Sorie, an older herder in a woven cone hat, sits on a low wooden stool beside a calm brown-and-white dairy cow and milks her by hand into a clean steel bucket.

Musa holds out a leafy branch to two friendly goats, one white and one brown, in the farmyard. In the corner a snail pen holds snails on fresh leaves, and a grasscutter looks out from its small wooden cage.

groups.title: Feed and animal health
groups.description: Feed, fodder, herbal remedies, pigs and pasture.

picture.alt: Pa Sorie in his woven cone hat adds an armful of fresh green fodder to a wooden feed trough where a dairy cow is eating. Mr Bangura, the extension officer, points to his clipboard notes on feeding and animal health. A feed sack and a jar of herbal remedy stand nearby.

groups.title: Crops
groups.description: Not in this bag yet. Ask your facilitator.

picture.alt: A green farm with rows of young rice, tall cassava plants and low groundnut plants, with palm trees behind. Kemoh walks between the rows carrying a hoe on his shoulder.
In the rain, Pa Foday in his straw hat bends to plant rice seedlings in the flooded swamp field, while Musa stands on the earth bank beside him holding a bundle of seedlings ready for him.

On a rainy day, flood volunteer Idrissa in an orange vest stands higher up the hill and points the way. Ya Sento walks up the path with her stick, and Hawa holds Musa's hand as they follow him to higher ground, away from the rising river and the house below.

groups.title: Keeping our land and water clean

picture.alt: Beside a stream under a big cotton tree, Hawa in her green climate-club T-shirt bends to pick up a plastic bottle from the bank and her friend Musa holds a sack open for the rubbish, so the water stays clean.
On a very hot, sunny day, Mama Kumba stands in the cool shade of a big mango tree and hands a cup of water to Musa, who reaches out to take it. A bucket of drinking water sits beside them.

blocks.text: Talking about safety at home
[Sample text] Children feel safe when they know they can talk to you about anything, big or small. This note gives you a few simple ways to start.
Choose a calm, ordinary moment to talk, for example while you cook or walk to the market. Short talks, often, work better than one big talk.
Get down to your child’s height. Look at them and listen.
Three things you can do this week

items: Use the real names for parts of the body, so your child can tell you clearly if something is wrong.
Agree on trusted adults. Your child can come to you, and to two more grown-ups you both trust.
Listen calmly. If your child tells you something, stay calm and say: “Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing.”

blocks.text: If you are ever worried about a child, you do not have to handle it alone. The Get help page shows who you can talk to.

questions.prompt: Why do we build the quail house off the ground?

answers.text: To keep the birds dry and safe
answers.feedback: A raised house stays dry when it rains, and it is harder for rats and snakes to get in.

answers.text: So the quail can fly out
answers.feedback: The house is raised to keep the birds dry and safe, not to let them out.
A raised house uses more wood, but it keeps the birds dry and safe.

questions.prompt: What helps quail stay healthy in their house?

answers.text: Fresh air, shade and a dry floor
answers.feedback: Fresh air, shade and a dry floor keep quail cool, clean and healthy.

answers.text: Full sun all day and no roof
answers.feedback: Good try. Too much sun makes quail too hot. Think about what keeps them cool and dry.

answers.text: A wet floor and closed walls
answers.feedback: Good try. A wet floor makes quail sick and closed walls stop fresh air.

questions.prompt: [Sample] What should quail always have in their house?

answers.feedback: Clean water and feed every day keep the birds strong.

answers.text: Nothing. They find food by themselves
answers.feedback: Quail in a house cannot look for food. They need you to bring it.
